track.title: Accounting 201
track.summary: Accrual accounting, adjusting entries, inventory, cash flow classification, internal controls, and closing.

orientationEssays.title: Why accrual accounting exists
orientationEssays.plainLanguageSummary: Accrual accounting separates when cash moves from when economic activity really happens. That distinction makes records more useful for judging performance.
orientationEssays.historicalOrigin: As trade and credit became more complex, cash receipts alone stopped telling the truth. Merchants needed records for promises, obligations, inventory, and timing.
orientationEssays.socialImportance: Accrual accounting helps lenders, owners, managers, and workers see whether a business is actually earning money or only temporarily holding cash.
orientationEssays.whyLearnersCare: A college senior should be able to tell the difference between being paid, earning revenue, owing money, and using up resources.
commonObjections: Learners often think profit should always equal cash.
Adjusting entries can feel artificial until the timing problem is visible.
deeperPaths: Study revenue recognition and matching in real company statements.
Compare cash-basis books with accrual-basis books for the same business.

concepts.title: Accrual vs Cash Basis
concepts.summary: Revenue and expenses should often be recognized when earned or incurred, not only when cash changes hands.
objectives: Classify a scenario as cash-basis or accrual-basis recognition.

diagnostics.prompt: A company performs $900 of services in March and receives cash in April. Under accrual accounting, which month records revenue?

practice.prompt: Rent for June is owed but unpaid on June 30. Under accrual accounting, should the expense be recognized in June or July?
hints: Ask when the resource was used, not when cash was paid.

feedback.correct: Correct. The expense belongs to the period that used the rent.
feedback.incorrect: Accrual accounting records the expense when incurred, even before cash payment.

evidenceRequired: Separates earning revenue from receiving cash.
Separates incurring expenses from paying cash.

items.prompt: A customer pays in advance for work that will happen next month. Is the first entry revenue or unearned revenue?
hints: The company has cash, but has not done the work yet.

feedback.correct: Correct. The business owes future service.
feedback.incorrect: Cash received before work is done is a liability until earned.

misconceptions.description: Learner treats cash receipt as the only moment revenue can exist.

remediation.message: Separate the promise, the work, the invoice, and the cash receipt.

sourceReferences.title: Curriculum scope
sourceReferences.note: Accounting 201 starts with accrual vs cash basis.

concepts.title: Adjusting Entries
concepts.summary: Period-end entries update revenue, expenses, assets, and liabilities so statements reflect economic reality.
objectives: Record simple accrued expense, deferred revenue, prepaid expense, and depreciation adjustments.

diagnostics.prompt: Record $300 of wages earned by employees but unpaid at month end.

checker.transaction: Record $300 of accrued wages at month end.

practice.prompt: Record $120 of insurance used from a prepaid insurance asset.
hints: The asset is being used up and expense is increasing.

feedback.correct: Correct. The adjustment moves used value from asset to expense.
feedback.incorrect: Prepaid Insurance decreases with a credit.

evidenceRequired: Records an adjustment without incorrectly using cash.
Explains how the adjustment changes statements.

items.prompt: Record $400 of services now earned from previously unearned revenue.

checker.transaction: Record $400 of previously unearned revenue now earned.

hints: Cash was received earlier; this adjustment recognizes earned revenue now.

feedback.correct: Correct. The liability goes down and revenue is earned.
feedback.incorrect: Do not record cash again when only the earning status changed.

misconceptions.description: Learner credits or debits cash in accrual adjustments even when no cash moves.

remediation.message: Ask whether cash actually moved today before using the Cash account.

sourceReferences.title: Curriculum scope
sourceReferences.note: Adjusting entries are the core Accounting 201 deterministic practice area.

concepts.title: Cash Flow Classification
concepts.summary: Cash flows are grouped into operating, investing, and financing activities so cash reality can be compared with profit.
objectives: Classify common cash flows as operating, investing, or financing.

diagnostics.prompt: A company receives cash from issuing a bank loan. Is this operating, investing, or financing cash flow?

practice.prompt: A company buys equipment for cash. Is this operating, investing, or financing cash flow?
hints: Equipment is a long-term productive asset.

feedback.correct: Correct. Buying long-term assets is investing activity.
feedback.incorrect: Operating cash flow is for core business operations, not buying long-term assets.

evidenceRequired: Classifies cash movements by business purpose.

items.prompt: A company pays dividends to owners. Is this operating, investing, or financing cash flow?
hints: Dividends are transactions with capital providers.

feedback.correct: Correct. Dividends are financing cash flows.
feedback.incorrect: Payments to owners belong with financing activities.

misconceptions.description: Learner treats every cash movement as operating cash flow.

remediation.message: Classify cash by why it moved: operations, long-term assets, or capital providers.

sourceReferences.title: Curriculum scope
sourceReferences.note: Cash flow classification is a required Accounting 201 target.
